title: Updating parameters
goals: Apply a learning rate to an ordered gradient
Update all parameters from the same saved state
Verify the new loss and identify overshooting

prerequisite.prompt: For x = 2, target 3, w = 1 and b = 0, what is the squared-loss gradient in order [w, b]?
prerequisite.answer: The residual is -1 and the gradient is [-4, -2].

vocabulary: A multiplier that controls the size of a gradient update
Updating parameters in the direction opposite the gradient
Computing all new parameter values from the same old state
A step that moves too far and can increase the objective

blocks.text: Gradient descent uses new parameter = old parameter - learning rate times its gradient entry. The minus sign chooses the locally downhill direction for a positive learning rate. A negative gradient therefore increases the corresponding parameter.

Keep the Week 10 example: x = 2, target 3, y = 2w + b and L = (y - 3) squared. At [w, b] = [1, 0], the loss is 1 and gradient is [-4, -2]. With learning rate 0.1, new w = 1 - 0.1 times -4 = 1.4 and new b = 0 - 0.1 times -2 = 0.2.
This particular step reaches zero loss on one example. It does not establish a unique parameter solution, successful learning on other examples or a generally ideal learning rate.

lesson.title: Save the old state before assignment

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: Predict the rows: unchanged parameters and loss 1 at rate 0; [1.2, 0.1] and loss 0.25 at rate 0.05; [1.4, 0.2] and loss 0 at rate 0.1; [2.2, 0.6] and loss 4 at rate 0.3. The helper performs one step on this fixed example; it assumes numeric inputs and does not choose a learning rate for you.

blocks.title: Use one gradient for one parameter snapshot
blocks.caption: Read top to bottom. All gradient entries come from the same old model. The final row evaluates the fully updated model rather than mixing old and new coordinates.

blocks.label: Starting again from [1, 0], use learning rate 0.05. Show both new parameters, the new prediction and the new loss.

blocks.text: Suppose a program first changes w to 1.4, then recomputes the bias gradient using new w and old b. Its residual is now -0.2, so its bias gradient is -0.4 and new b becomes 0.04. Prediction becomes 2.84 and loss 0.0256. That is a different procedure from the declared simultaneous step, even though it also lowered this loss.

An excessive rate can increase loss. At rate 0.3, both coordinates move in the locally suggested direction but prediction jumps to 5 and loss rises from 1 to 4. Always evaluate and record the result. Later lessons compare learning-rate behaviour across repeated updates.

A lower loss after a step supports progress on the objective and examples used for that step. It does not show that a model is safe, calibrated or better on unseen data. Keep the data split fixed and never use final-test labels to compute training gradients.

blocks.label: A teammate says any update that lowers loss is a correct implementation of simultaneous gradient descent. Use the mixed-state example to evaluate that claim.

blocks.text: Next week repeats the forward, loss, gradient and update cycle in a small network with a clearly stated stopping budget.

workbook.title: Apply a negative gradient
workbook.prompt: Starting with parameter a = 2, gradient -3 and learning rate 0.2, calculate the new a.

workbook.title: Detect overshooting
workbook.prompt: For the lesson start [1, 0], apply rate 0.3 and calculate prediction and loss.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Gradient [-4, -2] gives [2.2, 0.6], prediction 5 and loss 4, larger than the starting loss 1.

workbook.title: Preserve one snapshot
workbook.prompt: Explain why recomputing the bias gradient after changing w is not the simultaneous update specified here.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The two gradient entries then belong to different parameter vectors. Save the full old gradient and use it for both assignments.

workbook.title: Update a new model independently
workbook.prompt: Use x = 1, target 4, w = 1, b = 1, squared loss and learning rate 0.1. Compute prediction, residual, gradient [2 times residual times x, 2 times residual], new parameters and new loss.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Prediction 2, residual -2, gradient [-4, -4]. New parameters [1.4, 1.4] give prediction 2.8, residual -1.2 and loss 1.44, down from 4.

workbook.title: Evaluate a zero gradient
workbook.prompt: At a point with gradient [0, 0], what does this update do? Does that alone prove a global minimum on any loss surface?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It leaves parameters unchanged for a finite learning rate. Zero gradient alone does not establish a global minimum; stationary points can have other meanings.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions and keep old and new parameter boxes separate. This lesson checks one update, not a full optimiser. Treat the mixed-state procedure as different from the stated algorithm, rather than claiming all sequential methods are invalid.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the Week 10 gradient and write the update rule with parentheses around negative entries.
Calculate the rate 0.1 worked step and recompute the loss from the new parameters.
Complete W1 and the guided rate 0.05 calculation.
Run or trace all four code rows and complete W2.
Rebuild the old-state snapshot and compare it with the mixed-state example.
Complete W3 and discuss zero gradient with W5.
Collect W4 independently, including old loss, both new parameters and new loss.
Use the exit response and a fresh retry. Keep the model-quality claim separate from implementation correctness.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: [1.2, 0.1] gives prediction 2.5, residual -0.5 and loss 0.25. Exit: no. The mixed-state procedure lowers this loss but does not implement the specified simultaneous gradient step; compare states and gradients, not just whether loss decreased.
misconceptions: Subtracting a negative gradient decreases the parameter
Subtracting a negative adds a positive amount; show the signed calculation.
A downhill direction allows any rate
A finite step can overshoot and increase loss.
Recompute each gradient after its assignment
For this algorithm, all entries are computed at the same saved state.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires gradient [-4, -4], parameters [1.4, 1.4] and loss 1.44. Fresh retry: x = 1, target 1, w = 1, b = 1, rate 0.25 gives residual 1, gradient [2, 2], new parameters [0.5, 0.5] and loss 0. Require both updates to use the original residual.
teacher.support: Use separate old, gradient and new columns. Extension: for the lesson example, show that the new residual is the old residual multiplied by (1 - 10 times rate). Explain why rates 0 and 0.2 preserve loss while 0.3 raises it for a nonzero residual.
